paragraphs: This paper investigates the shape of a neural network’s training objective by finding many places where its slope becomes zero. These stationary points include local minima, where nearby changes cannot lower the error, and saddle points, which can slope upward in some directions and downward in others. Distinguishing them helps describe what an optimization algorithm encounters during training.

The authors define a globally convergent homotopy method that produces stationary points sequentially for a multilayer perceptron trained with mean squared error. Instead of obtaining only one endpoint from a training run, the method exposes a larger collection of stationary configurations. They apply it to two test problems and recover substantial subsets of their stationary points.

The empirical findings suggest that saddle points greatly outnumber local minima and that even small neural network problems can admit very many solutions. The contribution is therefore both a method for exploring the error surface and evidence that seemingly simple learning tasks can have surprisingly complicated optimization geometry.
neurips-1996-488-solutions-to-the-xor-pr.tldr: A method for finding many stationary points reveals abundant saddle points and numerous solutions even in small neural networks.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether flexible predictive models reveal relationships in epidemiological data that simpler statistical methods might overlook. Its subject is the relationship between tobacco, alcohol, and cancer. Flexibility creates an opportunity to detect unexpected patterns, but it also makes it easier to fit accidental features of the available observations.

The study compares the predictive quality of neural networks and other flexible models on both real and artificial epidemiological data. Those two settings serve complementary purposes: the real data address the substantive application, while the artificial data test whether a method can discover complex structure when such structure is present. Effective control of overfitting is central to the comparison.

The results suggest that the real data contain no major unexpected complex features. At the same time, the Bayesian neural network methodology controls overfitting while retaining the ability to uncover complex patterns in artificial data. Together, these findings support using flexible models with regularization to investigate complexity without assuming that more elaborate relationships must exist.
neurips-1996-a-comparison-between-neural.tldr: Bayesian neural networks control overfitting while detecting artificial complexity, but reveal no major unexpected complexity in the real epidemiological data.

paragraphs: The paper addresses classification when examples are plentiful but labels are scarce or expensive. Medical images illustrate the problem: collecting features can be easier than obtaining expert judgments about their classes. The aim is to let unlabelled observations contribute to learning alongside a smaller labelled collection.

The proposed classifier models features and labels jointly through a mixture of experts. Its structure is equivalent to a radial basis function classifier, but its probabilistic formulation supports training by maximizing the likelihood of all available data. The authors develop two expectation-maximization algorithms that differ in how they handle the unlabelled portion of the training set.

A further implication is that incoming test examples can themselves supply additional unlabelled information. Learning and classification can therefore be combined when new data arrive, rather than treating training as permanently finished. Experiments on UC Irvine datasets report substantial performance gains over alternative approaches. The central contribution is a structure and training procedure that make unlabelled examples useful within the classification process.
neurips-1996-a-mixture-of-experts-classi.tldr: A probabilistic mixture of experts improves classification by learning jointly from labelled examples and unlabelled data, including incoming test examples.

paragraphs: This paper changes the role of a neural network within a speech recognizer that also uses a hidden Markov model. Conventional hybrid systems use the network to estimate posterior class probabilities. Here, the network instead learns outputs that preserve information about the classes presented during training.

A special learning procedure maximizes mutual information between input classes and the sequence of output neurons that fire. The authors show that the resulting network acts as an optimal neural vector quantizer for a discrete hidden Markov model trained by maximum likelihood. In this role, the network converts inputs into discrete representations suitable for the sequence model.

The design matters because these networks can be combined with hidden Markov models of varying complexity, including models that account for context. The reported recognition rates reach the level of the best conventional continuous-parameter hidden Markov systems in the comparison. The authors also state that the network’s capabilities remain incompletely exploited, presenting the results as a strong demonstration of the approach’s potential.
neurips-1996-a-new-approach-to-hybrid-hm.tldr: Mutual-information training turns a neural network into a discrete representation builder for a competitive hybrid speech recognizer.

paragraphs: A hierarchical mixture of experts organizes multiple predictors into a hierarchy. Its structure determines how many experts are available and how they are arranged. This paper treats that structure as something to adapt during learning, proposing an automatic procedure that both grows the hierarchy and prunes it.

The constructive approach makes it possible to train large hierarchies containing several hundred experts effectively. Growth and pruning provide a way to change the model’s organization instead of committing in advance to a fixed, balanced structure. This makes the choice of architecture part of the learning procedure and provides a practical route to larger expert systems.

The authors evaluate the method on vowel classification and within a hybrid JANUS speech recognizer using a subset of the Switchboard database. They report better generalization than traditional static, balanced hierarchies. The finding supports the idea that how experts are organized matters alongside their individual training: an automatically developed hierarchy can predict new examples better than the fixed structures used in these comparisons.
neurips-1996-adaptively-growing-hierarch.tldr: Automatically growing and pruning expert hierarchies enables large models and improves generalization over fixed, balanced structures.

paragraphs: The paper studies an online classifier that learns only when it makes a mistake. On each trial it produces a binary decision using a linear threshold, and a correct prediction leaves its internal state unchanged. The algorithm is derived from a Bayesian learning procedure but changes when learning updates occur.

Its computational cost is linear in the number of attributes available to the learner. That property is important to the paper’s argument: the authors seek useful learning behavior without requiring a more expensive Bayesian computation. They examine the mistake-driven variant through both theoretical analysis and simulations, rather than relying only on its relationship to the original algorithm.

The results show good performance under assumptions substantially different from those encoded in the original Bayesian prior. The method also handles situations for which the authors do not know a linear-time Bayesian solution. The broader contribution is a demonstration that modifying a Bayesian-inspired update procedure can produce an efficient learner with useful behavior beyond the assumptions that originally motivated it.
neurips-1996-an-apobayesian-relative-of-.tldr: A mistake-driven Bayesian-inspired classifier learns efficiently and performs well beyond the assumptions of its original prior.

paragraphs: Separating speakers recorded by several microphones involves more than undoing a simple mixture. Sound reaches microphones with delays and is altered by the room, so each recording contains temporally spread versions of the sources. This paper studies how to separate those signals without already knowing the mixing process.

The authors develop natural-gradient information-maximization learning rules for recurrent networks with infinite impulse responses. These rules jointly adjust delays, separate sources, and undo convolution. They work well on simulated data, but fail in real rooms because room transfer functions commonly have a non-minimum-phase structure that stable filters of this kind cannot invert.

The paper then uses a feedforward architecture operating in the frequency domain to sidestep that obstacle. Information maximization in this representation enables a demonstration separating two natural signals recorded in a real room. The result highlights a concrete connection between model architecture and physical acoustics: success on simulated mixtures does not remove the need to accommodate the invertibility properties of actual room responses.
neurips-1996-blind-separation-of-delayed.tldr: Frequency-domain feedforward separation overcomes an acoustic inversion obstacle that defeats the paper’s recurrent approach in real rooms.

paragraphs: Combining several classifiers can reduce prediction error, but the benefit depends on how their mistakes line up. If committee members repeatedly misclassify the same examples, averaging their outputs has less opportunity to help. This paper focuses on reducing that shared pattern of errors while considering the accuracy of the individual networks.

The proposed training method introduces competition among committee members through a winner-take-all procedure. Its purpose is to push individual networks toward different minima in the space of weights that determine their predictions. Rather than treating each member’s training as unrelated to the rest of the committee, the procedure actively encourages different learned solutions.

The intended consequence is lower correlation between the networks’ errors on new examples, which reduces the committee’s combined error. The contribution connects a property of training—reaching different weight configurations—with the diversity needed for useful averaging. It explains why committee design involves more than assembling several individually capable classifiers: their errors must also leave room for one another to compensate.
neurips-1996-competition-among-networks-.tldr: Competitive training encourages committee members to reach different solutions and make less correlated errors.

paragraphs: This paper examines neural networks as distributions over possible functions. A prior distribution on network weights induces preferences over the functions the network can represent. For a broad class of weight priors, increasing the number of hidden units without bound makes that distribution over functions approach a Gaussian process.

The practical question is how to calculate with this limiting model. The authors derive analytic covariance functions for networks with sigmoidal hidden units and networks with Gaussian hidden units. A covariance function describes how function values at different inputs vary together, providing the information needed to work with the corresponding Gaussian process.

These formulas make efficient prediction possible for the infinite-hidden-unit limit. The apparent paradox is that an infinitely large network can become easier to compute with once its behavior is expressed through a covariance function. The contribution therefore turns a limiting theoretical relationship into a usable calculation: predictions can be obtained through the function distribution without explicitly representing an infinite collection of hidden units.
neurips-1996-computing-with-infinite-net.tldr: Analytic Gaussian-process covariance functions make prediction with certain infinite neural networks computationally practical.

paragraphs: Visual speechreading uses visible speech movements to help identify spoken words. This paper systematically compares ways to represent changes across video frames, asking which visual features support better recognition. It examines both how images are prepared and how their changing content is represented and compressed.

Normalizing images to remove differences in position, size, and rotation within the image plane substantially improves generalization across the representations tested. This result makes image alignment a central finding of the comparison. Changes caused by framing can interfere with the useful speech signal, so controlling those variations helps the recognition system work on new examples.

Two further comparisons favor relatively direct processing choices. Differences between consecutive frames outperform optical-flow representations, and local low-pass filtering outperforms global principal components analysis for compression. Together, the results show that a more elaborate motion description or global compression method need not yield better speechreading. The paper examines these outcomes and possible explanations, with the strongest conclusions tied to the representations actually compared.
neurips-1996-dynamic-features-for-visual.tldr: Image normalization, consecutive-frame differences, and local filtering perform strongly in a systematic visual speechreading comparison.

paragraphs: A controller can learn a model of a changing system and use dynamic programming to choose actions. The simplest version treats the learned model as correct, even though its predictions may be uncertain. This paper asks how estimates of that uncertainty can help when catastrophic failures must be prevented during learning.

The proposed algorithm draws on dual control and combines Bayesian locally weighted regression models with dynamic programming. The regression models provide uncertainty estimates alongside their fitted behavior. Those estimates give the controller information about where its knowledge is weak, making uncertainty relevant to action selection rather than merely a description of model quality.

The problem deliberately calls for restrained exploration: trying unfamiliar actions can carry unacceptable consequences. The algorithm is illustrated on a simulated control task with four dimensions. Its contribution is an approach to using model uncertainty in the learning-and-control process when gathering experience must be balanced against avoiding failure, rather than assuming that aggressive exploration is always desirable.
neurips-1996-exploiting-model-uncertaint.tldr: A control-learning algorithm uses Bayesian model uncertainty to restrain exploration when failures could be catastrophic.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a biologically motivated model for how useful representations can organize themselves. Its central idea is to combine immediate, bottom-up information with context, allowing the model to learn features that remain meaningful as observations change. The combination is expressed through a maximum-likelihood objective.

Groups containing one or more units share a contextual gating signal that modulates their activity. Through learning, the units become mutually supportive predictors of abstract contextual features. Shared modulation gives context an organizing role: it influences how groups of units develop their representations, rather than leaving each unit to respond only to the current bottom-up input.

The authors test whether the model can discover classes that stay consistent across viewpoints using real image sequences of centered faces rotating gradually. With few training examples, it generalizes to unseen views considerably better than supervised backpropagation. The result supports the value of contextual organization for this setting, where changing images contain persistent class information and the training sequences expose that continuity.
neurips-1996-learning-temporally-persist.tldr: Contextually gated groups learn representations that generalize across unseen face views from few training examples.

paragraphs: Learning from sequences becomes difficult when a relevant input and the feedback needed to learn from it are separated by many steps. This paper examines both algorithms for that problem and the benchmarks used to judge them. It argues that a long delay alone does not establish that a task is a demanding test of learning.

The authors first show that problems used to support several earlier methods can be solved faster by randomly guessing network weights. Their random-search procedure repeatedly initializes a network and tests it until it finds a solution. In their terminology, a task is trivial if this procedure succeeds quickly, even when the sequence contains a long time lag.

They then apply LSTM to a harder problem that random search cannot solve quickly and that no other recurrent-network algorithm known to them can quickly solve. The contribution combines a positive result for LSTM with a methodological point: sequence benchmarks should distinguish effective learning from success that can be obtained through simple weight guessing.
neurips-1996-lstm-can-solve-hard-long-ti.tldr: LSTM solves a demanding long-delay task after random weight search exposes weaknesses in earlier benchmarks.

paragraphs: The paper studies neural network learning through equations that describe individual examples. For a given example, it relates the field involved in aligning the network with that example to a cavity field: the corresponding field when that example is left out of learning. This comparison connects an example’s influence to the system formed by the remaining data.

The analysis addresses a rough energy landscape containing multiple local minima. It assumes that the density of those minima follows an exponential distribution. Under that assumption, the resulting large-scale properties agree with a first-step replica symmetry breaking solution, linking the example-level equations to a broader statistical description of the learning system.

The equations also supply a computational procedure: repeatedly applying them produces a learning algorithm. The authors report that this algorithm achieves higher stability than conventional algorithms. The contribution therefore joins theory and training, using a specific assumption about the landscape’s local minima to derive equations that both reproduce macroscopic behavior and guide iterative learning.
neurips-1996-microscopic-equations-in-ro.tldr: Example-level equations connect a rough learning landscape to statistical theory and yield an algorithm with higher reported stability.

paragraphs: This paper improves a controller’s decisions by simulating what could happen after each available action. A starting policy supplies the decisions made later in each simulated trajectory. By repeating these simulations, the algorithm estimates the long-term expected reward associated with each candidate action and selects the one with the highest estimate.

The procedure uses an existing policy as the basis for real-time improvement. Its simulations are readily parallelized, and the authors implement it on IBM SP1 and SP2 parallel computers. The approach is potentially applicable to other control problems where the environment can be simulated, because its action comparisons depend on those simulated futures.

Initial backgammon results cover starting policies ranging from random play to the strong neural-network player TD-Gammon. Every tested starting policy benefits, with reported error-rate reductions reaching a factor of five or more. The findings show that simulation-based lookahead can improve both weak and strong decision rules by evaluating their longer-term consequences at the moment an action is needed.
neurips-1996-on-line-policy-improvement-.tldr: Monte Carlo lookahead substantially improves backgammon policies by comparing simulated long-term rewards before each decision.

paragraphs: Programs create objects in dynamically allocated memory, and those objects remain useful for different lengths of time. Predicting their lifetimes can help memory management use both time and space more efficiently. This paper builds on earlier work that demonstrated those benefits with a simple lifetime predictor across several programs.

The authors replace that predictor with decision trees and evaluate prediction on the same programs. A decision tree bases its output on a sequence of feature-dependent choices. The reported result is significantly better lifetime prediction, establishing an improvement in the information that a memory-management strategy could use when deciding how to handle allocated objects.

A second advantage concerns feature selection. During training, the method can consider many features and let the tree choose a relevant subset automatically. That reduces the need to decide in advance which available signals should drive the predictor. The contribution is therefore a more accurate prediction method with built-in selection of useful inputs; the stated new result concerns prediction quality, while the efficiency motivation comes from the earlier memory-management work.
neurips-1996-predicting-lifetimes-in-dyn.tldr: Decision trees improve memory-object lifetime prediction while automatically selecting relevant features from a larger candidate set.

paragraphs: This paper develops theoretical guarantees for learning nonlinear functions with a radial basis function network containing one hidden layer. Training uses complexity regularization together with empirical risk minimization. The goal is to connect the model’s fit to observed data with bounds on the prediction loss expected beyond that sample.

The analysis uses random covering numbers and metric entropy, mathematical tools for measuring how large or varied a family of candidate functions is. This formulation accommodates a broader family of activation functions, specifically functions of bounded variation. It also removes some restrictions that earlier approaches imposed on network parameters, extending the range of networks covered by the theory.

The authors derive expected-risk bounds that depend on sample size for a broad class of loss functions. They also establish rates at which the risk approaches the optimal loss. These results explain how increasing the amount of data relates to learning accuracy under the proposed regularization framework, while broadening the mathematical conditions under which such guarantees can be obtained.
neurips-1996-radial-basis-function-netwo.tldr: Complexity regularization yields learning guarantees for radial basis function networks under broader activation and parameter conditions.

paragraphs: Regression often describes observations as a predictable function plus random noise. A common assumption is that this noise is Gaussian and has the same variance at every input. Under that model, maximum-likelihood fitting is equivalent to minimizing the sum of squared prediction errors, giving a familiar justification for least-squares training.

The paper considers the more flexible case in which noise variance changes with the input. That allows some parts of the input space to have more variable target values than others. Modeling this variation matters because a single noise level cannot express differences in how tightly observations follow the underlying function across different inputs.

The authors identify a problem with applying maximum likelihood to this richer model: it can produce highly biased results. They show that a Bayesian treatment can accommodate input-dependent variance while overcoming that bias. The contribution is therefore about both the noise model and how it is fitted. Allowing variable noise requires an estimation method suited to that additional flexibility.
neurips-1996-regression-with-input-depen.tldr: A Bayesian approach models noise that changes with the input while overcoming the bias of maximum-likelihood fitting.

paragraphs: Feedback control usually assumes that observing the system is free. This paper studies the case where sensing has a cost, so it can be worthwhile to execute several actions before observing again. The learner must decide how to combine closed-loop behavior using current feedback with open-loop behavior between observations.

The sensors are assumed reliable, but skipping observations still makes the current state uncertain. The algorithm therefore uses short-term memory to handle this particular hidden-state problem. Memory supports decisions when fresh sensory information is unavailable, making the choice to sense part of the control problem rather than an automatic step before every action.

The main contribution is a pruning rule that sharply restricts exploration of possible memory states. It prunes states where the estimated value of obtaining information exceeds the cost of that information, identifying circumstances in which sensing is worthwhile. The authors prove that this rule preserves convergence to an optimal policy. Thus, the method reduces the memory-related search while retaining the stated optimality guarantee.
neurips-1996-reinforcement-learning-for-.tldr: A reinforcement learner balances sensing costs against acting without feedback, with a memory-pruning rule that preserves optimal-policy convergence.

paragraphs: Disparity estimation combines local evidence about positional differences between corresponding image content. That evidence can be sparse and noisy, creating a tension: averaging helps stabilize estimates, but averaging across a boundary can merge distinct disparities. The paper develops a network that chooses which local estimates to combine.

The model uses disparity-selective units inspired by early visual processing and a selection mechanism that integrates reliable local information. It combines processing at multiple image scales with mixture-of-experts learning. This arrangement allows the model to estimate more than one disparity within a region, accommodating cases involving transparency or occlusion rather than forcing every region into a single estimate.

Tests on real images and random-dot stereograms show accurate multiple-disparity estimation and better performance than standard backpropagation and cross-correlation approaches. The learned representations also agree with reported physiological findings for cells in visual area V2. The contribution links an effective computational principle—selecting compatible evidence before combining it—with a model whose internal representations have stated connections to biological vision.
neurips-1996-selective-integration-a-mod.tldr: Selective integration improves disparity estimation by combining reliable local evidence without merging distinct disparities.

paragraphs: Relational graph matching seeks correspondences that respect the structure of two graphs. This paper starts from a Bayesian consistency measure that evaluates structural differences using Hamming distance. Such a measure provides a way to score disagreement, but its discrete components create a matching problem expressed through distinct choices.

The authors show how to soften those discrete components of the cost function. This changes the mathematical representation of the matching objective so that continuous nonlinear optimization can be used to locate matches. The key contribution is the connection between a discrete structural score and a form that can be handled by continuous optimization methods.

The paper also establishes how the resulting matching algorithm relates to the standard quadratic assignment problem. That connection places the proposed procedure alongside an established mathematical formulation of assignment with relational costs. Taken together, the contributions form a coherent framework: begin with a probabilistic consistency score, soften its discrete terms, and use the transformed objective to search for graph correspondences.
neurips-1996-softening-discrete-relaxati.tldr: Softening a discrete graph-matching objective enables continuous optimization and connects the resulting method to quadratic assignment.

paragraphs: This paper explores automated detection of cervical precancer from fluorescence spectra measured in living tissue. The motivation is early detection: the abstract identifies difficulty achieving both high sensitivity and high specificity with existing detection techniques. A useful detector must recognize affected tissue while also distinguishing it from tissue that should not be classified as precancerous.

Fluorescence spectroscopy provides a rapid, noninvasive, quantitative way to probe biochemical and morphological changes in tissue. The proposed system applies ensembles of radial basis function networks to those measurements. The networks turn spectral information into a detection result, linking a physical measurement of tissue properties with an automated classification procedure.

The authors describe near-real-time operation suitable for use by nonexperts and report more reliable, direct, and accurate results than those obtained by human experts or multivariate statistical algorithms in their comparison. The contribution is the combination of spectroscopy and neural-network ensembles for accessible automated detection, with the reported advantage arising from how the spectral evidence is interpreted.
neurips-1996-spectroscopic-detection-of-.tldr: Radial basis function ensembles interpret fluorescence spectra for rapid automated cervical precancer detection with reported comparative accuracy gains.

paragraphs: This paper studies how a mixture of experts develops useful specialization as the number of training examples increases. The analysis assumes that examples come from another network with the same architecture. Within this matched setting, it examines when the learner’s experts begin taking on distinct roles and how that relates to generalization.

Below a critical number of examples, the system remains in a symmetric phase: its experts have not specialized. Once the sample size crosses that point, a continuous phase transition occurs. The gating network begins dividing the input space effectively, and each expert becomes associated with an appropriate part of that space.

For mixtures with multiple hierarchical levels, the authors find multiple phase transitions. This means the emergence of organization can involve more than one transition as data accumulate. The contribution provides a statistical-mechanics account of specialization: simply including several experts does not ensure distinct responsibilities, and sufficient training evidence is needed for the division of labor to emerge in the studied setting.
neurips-1996-statistical-mechanics-of-th.tldr: A mixture of experts begins specializing after a critical sample size, with multiple transitions appearing in hierarchical models.

paragraphs: This paper investigates why gradient descent can learn slowly when input variables are correlated. It studies a linear perceptron, a setting where convergence can be analyzed through a response function. The authors derive a general expression for that function and use it to examine data with simple forms of input correlation.

The analysis shows that correlations can severely slow learning. This supplies an explanation for the effectiveness of principal components analysis in reducing training time: the organization of the inputs affects the dynamics of optimization. The result makes preprocessing relevant to how quickly learning proceeds, rather than treating the training algorithm as the sole determinant of convergence.

Motivated by the theory, the authors propose removing means across both input variables and examples to decrease correlations. Numerical results on a medical classification problem agree closely with the theoretical findings. The paper therefore connects an analytical account of slow convergence with a concrete data transformation and an application that supports the predicted relationship between correlation and learning speed.
neurips-1996-the-effect-of-correlated-in.tldr: An analysis of linear-perceptron learning shows how input correlations slow gradient descent and motivates correlation-reducing preprocessing.

paragraphs: The Neurothermostat controls residential heating by deciding when to switch a furnace on or off. Its objective combines occupant comfort with energy cost. Because heating decisions have delayed effects, the controller must anticipate demand using predictions of occupancy and of how the house and furnace respond thermally.

Occupancy prediction combines a neural network with a lookup table. At each decision time, the controller searches for a sequence of furnace actions that minimizes expected cost over a fixed future horizon. It executes the first action and then repeats the search, continually updating its plan rather than committing to the entire sequence at once.

The authors test the controller in simulations using artificial occupancy patterns with varied regularity and occupancy data from a real residence. It achieves consistently lower costs than three conventional policies. The advantage persists across different comfort-versus-energy weightings and levels of occupancy variability. These findings support predictive control that learns household patterns and uses them to coordinate heating with expected need.
neurips-1996-the-neurothermostat-predict.tldr: The Neurothermostat predicts occupancy and thermal behavior to reduce combined comfort and energy costs in heating simulations.
